$comment: The starting outline of each book: where every required page of the template goes, under which title, and what the page has to contain. scaffold_docs.py reads it together with the validator's template.json; a page with an "id" is written only while template.json (or the project's .docs-template.json) still requires that id. {name} is replaced with the project name.

user.description: What {name} is and how to use it day to day.
user.audience: This guide is for anyone who uses {name}. It assumes no technical background.

card.title: User guide
card.summary: What {name} is and how to use it day to day, in plain words.
bullets: Everyday tasks, one at a time

user.readme_brief: Open with one bold sentence on what {name} does for the reader, then two or three short paragraphs in plain words. Keep the audience sentence, the reading-map table (one row per common need, not a copy of SUMMARY) and the pointer to the other books.

chapters.title: Quick start
chapters.brief: A timed walk-through from nothing to the first useful result. Say in the lead paragraph how long it takes, list what the reader needs first, then numbered steps with the exact command or click and what the reader should see after each. End with where to go next. Facts: the install instructions and the shortest working example in the repository; run the steps if you can.

chapters.title: Everyday use
chapters.brief: One H2 per common job, named by what the reader wants to do, each with the shortest way to do it and one example. Facts: the commands, screens or prompts the product offers; leave out anything only an operator needs.

chapters.title: Trust and privacy
chapters.want: Know what you can rely on
chapters.brief: What the reader can rely on, what the product reads and writes, what leaves the machine and what never does. Facts: network calls, files written, telemetry and permissions found in the code; state only what the code shows.

chapters.title: Use cases
chapters.brief: Three to five concrete stories: who, the problem, how {name} helps, what they do. Facts: examples in the repository, the README, issues; do not invent customers.

chapters.title: Questions and troubleshooting
chapters.brief: The page people land on when something breaks. One H2 per question, phrased as the reader would ask it, or per symptom with the exact error text. Each answer: the cause in one sentence, then the fix. Facts: error messages in the code, known issues, the README.

chapters.title: Glossary
chapters.brief: Every project word this book uses, in alphabetical order, each defined in one or two plain sentences without using another glossary word. Only words that appear in this book.

operator.description: How {name} works inside, and how to install, configure, monitor and operate it.
operator.audience: This guide is for the people who install, configure and run {name}. It assumes you are comfortable with a terminal.
operator.blurb: covers how it works inside, installation, every setting, monitoring and operations
map_header: Read it when you need to…

card.title: Operator guide
card.summary: How {name} works inside, and how to install, configure, monitor and operate it.
bullets: How it works, install and deploy

operator.readme_brief: After the audience sentence, one paragraph that says what {name} is in an operator's terms (processes, storage, dependencies). Keep the reading-map table, add a Conventions section (how commands are shown, what project words mean), link design documents outside the docs root with absolute repository URLs, and keep the pointer to the other books.

chapters.title: How it works
chapters.when: Understand the parts of the system and how they fit together

pages.title: System overview
pages.brief: The runtime view every later chapter assumes: the processes or components that run, what each one owns, how a request or a piece of data moves through them, and where state is kept. A diagram helps. Stay at the level an operator can observe; the code layout belongs in the developer book when there is one. Facts: the entry points and the design documents.

pages.title: Install
pages.brief: Every supported way to install, each with prerequisites, the exact commands and how to verify the result. Then upgrading and uninstalling. Facts: the build files, release configuration, Dockerfile, package manifests and CI.

chapters.title: Configuration reference
chapters.when: Look up a setting, a command or a flag

pages.title: Environment variables and settings
pages.brief: A complete reference: one table row per setting with its name in backticks, type, default and effect. Complete means every setting the code reads; grep the code for them, do not work from memory. Quote the defaults from the code.

pages.title: Commands and flags
pages.brief: Every command and flag the binary accepts, each with a one-line purpose, its arguments and one example. Facts: the argument parser in the code or the --help output, not the README.

chapters.title: Monitoring
chapters.when: See what the system is doing and be told when it breaks

pages.title: Metrics and logs
pages.brief: Which signals exist (logs, metrics, health checks, traces), where each one appears, its format, and which ones deserve an alert. Facts: the logging and metrics calls in the code. If the product emits none, say so and say how an operator can tell that it is healthy.

chapters.title: Operations
chapters.when: Back up, repair, upgrade or troubleshoot

pages.title: Troubleshooting runbook
pages.brief: Day-two work. One H2 per symptom: how to confirm it, the likely causes in order, the fix, and how to check that it worked. Add backup and restore when the product keeps state. Facts: error paths in the code, data files, migration code.

pages.title: Glossary
pages.brief: Project-specific terms in alphabetical order, each defined precisely in one or two sentences, with the name it has in the code where that differs.

tester.description: How every change to {name} is checked, and how to run, read, explore and add tests.
tester.audience: This guide is for the people who check that changes to {name} are safe. It assumes you can run commands in a terminal and read a test report.
tester.blurb: explains how every change is checked
map_header: Read it when you need to…

card.title: Tester guide
card.summary: How every change is checked, and how to run, read, explore and add tests.
bullets: Running the tests and what is tested where
The gates that block a merge
Exploring by hand and adding tests

tester.readme_brief: After the audience sentence, one paragraph on how {name} is tested as a whole (which kinds of tests, what runs on every change). Keep the reading-map table, add a Conventions section (how commands and test names are shown) and keep the pointer to the other books.

chapters.title: Getting started
chapters.when: Run everything once and find the tests for an area

pages.title: Running the tests
pages.brief: How to run the whole suite once: prerequisites, the one command, how long it takes, what a pass and a failure look like, then how to run one package or one test. Facts: the Makefile or task runner, the test configuration and CI; run the command if you can.

pages.title: What is tested where
pages.brief: A table from product area to the test files that cover it and the kind of test, so a reviewer can find the tests for a change. Include the areas with no tests. Facts: the test files in the repository.

chapters.title: Automated gates
chapters.when: Know what blocks a merge and why

pages.title: Continuous integration
pages.brief: Every check that runs on a pull request: what it checks, the command that reproduces it locally, and whether it blocks the merge. Facts: the workflow files and the Makefile. If there is no CI, say so and list what a reviewer has to run by hand.

chapters.title: Exploratory testing
chapters.when: Look for what the automated tests miss

pages.title: Exploring by hand
pages.brief: How to set up a safe sandbox, which areas are worth probing, what to try in each and how to report what you find. Facts: the product's risky paths, such as input parsing, concurrency, upgrades and data loss.

chapters.title: Adding tests
chapters.when: Write the right test for a change

pages.title: Adding tests
pages.brief: Which kind of test to write for which kind of change, where the file goes, a minimal example copied from an existing test, and the pull-request checklist. Facts: the conventions the existing tests follow.

chapters.title: Appendix: words and commands
chapters.when: Look up a testing word or a command
chapters.brief: Testing vocabulary used in this book (for example golden, baseline, gate, fixture), each in one or two sentences, then a table of every test command with what it runs.

developer.description: How the code of {name} is organised, and how to build, change, extend and release it.
developer.audience: This guide is for the people who change the code of {name}. It assumes you know the language it is written in and can use git.
developer.blurb: explains how the code is organised and how to change it
map_header: Read it when you need to…

card.title: Developer guide
card.summary: How the code is organised, and how to build, change, extend and release it.

developer.readme_brief: After the audience sentence, one paragraph on what kind of code base this is (language, size, main dependencies) and what a typical change looks like. Keep the reading-map table, add a Conventions section (how paths, package and function names are shown) and keep the pointer to the other books.

chapters.title: How the code is organised
chapters.when: Find the code that does a thing

pages.title: Architecture and code layout
pages.brief: The code view: one row or section per package or module with what it owns and what it may call, the main data types, and the path of one typical request through the code, naming the functions. Say why the code is shaped this way where the reason is not obvious. Facts: the source tree and the imports; the operator book has the runtime view, so link to it instead of repeating it.

chapters.title: Development setup
chapters.when: Get from a fresh checkout to a running build

pages.title: Development environment
pages.brief: From a fresh checkout to a running build and a passing test run: required tools with versions, the exact commands in order, what each prints when it works, and how to run the product from the working tree. Facts: the build files, the lock files, the Makefile or task runner, CI; run the commands if you can.

chapters.title: Contributing
chapters.when: Make a change that will be merged

pages.title: Conventions and pull requests
pages.brief: The rules a change follows: code style and the tool that enforces it, naming, commit messages, how a pull request is reviewed and what CI checks. When there is no tester book, also say how to run the tests and which test a change needs. Facts: linter and formatter configuration, CI workflows, CONTRIBUTING, the history of the repository; state only rules that the repository shows.

chapters.title: Extending
chapters.when: Add behaviour without patching the core

pages.title: Extension points
pages.brief: The supported ways to add behaviour (a new command, handler, plugin, backend), each with the interface to implement, where to register it, and a minimal example taken from an existing one. If the code has no extension points, say so and describe how a typical feature is added instead.

pages.title: Release process
pages.brief: How a version is cut: where the version number lives, the steps in order, what is automated and what is manual, and how to check the published result. Facts: the release workflow, packaging configuration, tags in the repository. Do not describe a process the repository does not show.

chapters.title: Appendix: names in the code
chapters.when: Look up what a name in the code means
chapters.brief: Names used in the code (types, packages, abbreviations), in alphabetical order, each with one or two sentences and the name users and operators see when it differs.
